Towards a Systematic Study of Embodied System 2 over Full Task Execution Cycles

Yuxi Wei Ye Fang Shuai Yang Tong Wu Tai Wang Xiaojuan Qi The University of Hong Kong Morphi Robot Fudan University Shanghai Jiao Tong University *Co-corresponding authors
Abstract

An embodied brain, or System 2, must turn an abstract goal into actions while discovering relevant scene conditions and checking whether executed skills achieved their intended effects. Open-loop evaluations cannot test observations shaped by an agent’s decisions, while some closed-loop evaluations provide limited evidence during execution or assume idealized skill outcomes. We introduce SCOPER, a suite for studying observation-grounded planning, execution, and recovery. SCOPER-bench combines high-level goals, ongoing visual observations, a shared rule-based System 1 for low-level actions, and controlled execution failures. Its construction and validation pipeline yields 870 tasks across BEHAVIOR and ProcTHOR, complemented by about 3,500 situated questions tied to the evaluated agent’s execution. Benchmark results reveal difficulties in retaining scene evidence, monitoring progress, and recovering from unexpected outcomes. To address these difficulties, SCOPER-harness combines Evidence Memory and Progress Verification with a dynamic task agenda and bounded exploration, without additional model training. Across two evaluated open-source backbones and two simulators, the harness improves task success by 11.1–28.6%; a harnessed 9B model outperforms a directly executed 27B model on both simulators. In an offline next-action evaluation using observations from 200 real-robot demonstrations, the harness also improves full-call accuracy by 14.7% and 15.3%. SCOPER provides a setting for diagnosing and improving embodied reasoning throughout a complete task execution cycle.

Project website: https://vfishc.github.io/scoper/

1 Introduction

An embodied agent must do more than turn a goal into a sequence of actions (Huang et al., 2022b; Singh et al., 2022; Song et al., 2022). Its high-level controller, which we call the embodied brain or System 2, must decide what information to seek, interpret visual observations (Driess et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2022), select skills (Mu et al., 2023; Ahn et al., 2024), and determine whether those skills achieved their intended effects (Guo et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b). A low-level System 1 executes the selected skills, following the separation of language-based planning and skill execution explored in prior embodied systems (Ahn et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2022c; Liang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023). In a partially observed environment, exploration may reveal new requirements, while an unsuccessful action may invalidate the current plan (Guo et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b). These demands are coupled: what the agent observes shapes what it should do (Wu et al., 2023b; Wu et al., 2023a), and what happens after it acts shapes what it should do next. Studying them together is essential to understanding whether an embodied brain can guide long-horizon behavior through a complete closed-loop task (Yenamandra et al., 2023).

Figure 1 summarizes these demands and their treatment by SCOPER-bench and SCOPER-harness. Existing evaluations inadequately capture these coupled demands. Open-loop evaluations based on recorded egocentric videos assess interpretation of fixed observations (Qiu et al., 2024; Dang et al., 2025; Majumdar et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2022; Cheng et al., 2024), but cannot test whether an agent acquires missing evidence, adjusts task decomposition through interaction, or recovers from its own execution failures. Existing closed-loop benchmarks (Yang et al., 2025b; Cheng et al., 2025; Srivastava et al., 2021) also leave gaps when they omit intermediate execution observations, assume idealized execution, or provide detailed procedural instructions. These choices limit evaluation of evidence accumulation, outcome monitoring, and recovery, and can reduce planning to instruction-driven subtask sequencing with limited need for visual reasoning. The action–result loop alone therefore cannot establish conditions for studying embodied System 2.

We introduce the SCOPER suite for studying System 2 in closed-loop, observation-grounded planning, execution, and recovery, comprising SCOPER-bench and SCOPER-harness. SCOPER-bench requires agents to infer subtasks from abstract goals and multi-frame visual observations throughout execution; construction-time decompositions serve validation. A unified rule-based System 1 supplies shared execution infrastructure, and a scalable construction and validation pipeline yields 870 tasks across two simulators (Section 3). Controlled failure injection tests whether agents detect unmet expectations and replan to resume progress. Evaluations reveal persistent difficulties in acquiring and maintaining scene evidence for planning, monitoring outcomes, and recovering from failures.

SCOPER-harness addresses these difficulties through Evidence Memory, which maintains explicit language descriptions of observed scene information, and Progress Verification, which checks expected outcomes against observations after each execution step. A dynamic agenda organizes pending subtasks and is updated using accumulated evidence and verification results. Because repeated exploration and checking can delay execution, an anti-deadlock mechanism limits unproductive repetition to balance information gathering with task advancement.

Experiments show that complete execution remains challenging even with shared low-level skills: the strongest directly evaluated model achieves 50.5% task success on BEHAVIOR and 35.1% on ProcTHOR. Across evaluated open-source models, SCOPER-harness consistently improves performance, with gains of up to 28.6 percentage points, enabling a smaller model to perform comparably to the strongest evaluated model. Evaluated embodied-finetuned models also underperform general-purpose models, indicating that embodied specialization does not necessarily yield stronger closed-loop reasoning in this setting. Tests with real-world observations further show that benchmark-guided harness refinements improve performance, particularly in memory- dependent and failure-recovery cases.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) SCOPER-bench: A validated cross-simulator benchmark jointly testing observation-grounded task decomposition, execution, and failure recovery. (2) SCOPER-harness: A harness connecting scene evidence and verified outcomes to adaptive task agendas and sustained execution. (3) Experiments and findings: We identify gaps in scene evidence discovery and failure verification and design a targeted harness that consistently improves performance across evaluated models, with further gains on real-world observation tests.

2 Related Work

Open-loop Evaluation of Embodied Reasoning.

Recent benchmarks evaluate embodied understanding and planning from recorded egocentric observations by asking the models to answer some open-loop questions. (Grauman et al., 2021; Grauman et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2023; Mangalam et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025a). EgoPlan-Bench2 (Qiu et al., 2024) tests planning in everyday scenarios, and ECBench (Dang et al., 2025) examines diverse embodied cognitive abilities. These protocols probe reasoning over visual evidence, but observations remain independent of the evaluated model’s decisions. They therefore cannot establish whether an agent can acquire missing evidence through action, revise task decomposition as execution unfolds, or recover from its own execution failures. SCOPER-bench tests these demands through decision-dependent observations and outcome-guided planning and recovery.

Closed-loop Embodied Benchmarks.

Interactive benchmarks (Shridhar et al., 2019; Shridhar et al., 2020; Padmakumar et al., 2021; Puig et al., 2018) increasingly evaluate embodied agents through simulated task execution (Savva et al., 2019; Szot et al., 2021; Puig et al., 2023; Deitke et al., 2020; Mees et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023a). EmbodiedBench (Yang et al., 2025b) and EmbodiedEval (Cheng et al., 2025) extend evaluation to visual navigation, interaction, and planning, but their standard stepwise interfaces emphasize observations at action boundaries rather than evidence acquired within skill execution. Moreover, action-validity feedback does not systematically test whether agents detect and recover from deviations between intended and actual skill effects. BEHAVIOR (Srivastava et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Li et al., 2021) evaluates complex household activities through integrated planning and control, making high-level reasoning difficult to disentangle from low-level execution in end-to-end performance. SCOPER-bench isolates these System 2 demands using shared, controllable System 1 skills, multi-frame execution observations, explicit failure injection, and high-level goals.

Agentic designs for embodied intelligence.

Embodied frameworks combine planning, memory, and execution feedback to sustain long-horizon behavior (Rana et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a; Yao et al., 2022; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023b). Cortex (Peng et al., 2026) aligns VLM planning with VLA execution through standardized subtasks and semantic memory; Thea (Wang et al., 2026) integrates persistent scene context with action-outcome evaluation; Mimir (Xu et al., 2026) grounds an evolving task agenda in world memory and explores under insufficient evidence. SCOPER-harness emphasizes how scene discovery determines an abstract goal’s required work, coupling exploration, evidence-driven agenda revision, and verified progress (Section 4).

3 SCOPER-bench

We test System 2 information acquisition, goal decomposition, subtask selection, and plan revision from observations and outcomes. Instructions specify requirements, not action sequences; completion and situated question answering (QA) assess execution and scene/task understanding.

3.1 Task Formulation and Evaluation Protocol

Task groups.

We organize the benchmark into four groups. Routine execution specifies concrete task requirements while leaving action selection and sequencing to the agent. Observation-dependent covers state-dependent execution, scene inspection, and responses to task updates. Failure recovery covers initially present anomalies, controlled execution failures, and mid-execution disturbances that require corrective actions or replanning. Composite combines multiple subtasks, requiring agents to maintain progress and reason over cross-step dependencies; these subtasks can draw from the other three groups.

Observation-dependent decisions.

Tasks differ in their information needs before acting. For example, “put the cup in the cabinet” identifies the object and destination, whereas “inspect the room, clean the dishware that needs cleaning, and put it away” requires discovering which objects need attention. Observation remains necessary after acting: following a placement request, the agent must inspect whether the object reached its destination and assess further action needs.

Task representation.

A task instance is represented as 𝒯=(x,ℛ,𝒞0,𝒢,ℰ,𝒬)\mathcal{T}=(x,\mathcal{R},\mathcal{C}_{0},\mathcal{G},\mathcal{E},\mathcal{Q}), where xx is the instruction, ℛ\mathcal{R} specifies object-role constraints, 𝒞0\mathcal{C}_{0} defines initial conditions, 𝒢\mathcal{G} contains goal predicates, ℰ\mathcal{E} configures optional execution events, and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} contains attached questions. This configuration supports construction and evaluation. Evaluated System 2 uses instructions, visual observations, and prescribed public tool information; construction-time role bindings, reference decompositions, and privileged simulator state provide no planning guidance.

Agent inputs and evaluation protocol.

System 2 receives instructions, tool descriptions, permitted vocabulary, decision history, and tool-returned images. Exploration and navigation return eight uniformly sampled execution frames; state-changing actions return before-and-after frames. Direct execution retains up to 32 frames; harness context routing appears in Section 4.1 and Appendix J. Execution ends on stop or step-budget exhaustion. Success requires both stop and the resulting environment state satisfying the template’s goal predicates. Triggered questions use dedicated answer-only turns with the same context available to policy decisions. Observation settings, budgets, and scoring rules appear in Appendix A; QA activation and answering details appear in Appendix I.

3.2 Oracle System 1 and Controlled Execution

Unified skill infrastructure.

Oracle System 1 provides rule-based active observation, navigation, and manipulation skills shared by evaluated models and the construction-time teacher. Standardizing execution controls low-level variation without training a separate policy for each model. Complete skill definitions and object binding are given in Appendices E and H. Navigation uses A* search (Hart et al., 1968) over traversability maps derived from scene collision geometry. Manipulation bypasses low-level physical execution, directly updating object poses, holding or containment relations, and task-relevant states with synchronized visual representations. Navigation, scanning, and target search collect multi-frame observations along paths and viewpoints; state-changing actions expose their visual outcomes for subsequent System 2 decisions.

Controlled failures and perturbations.

Template-defined events alter System 1 behavior or outcomes at designated stages, requiring inspection of deviations, identification of unmet requirements, and recovery or replanning. This combines shared execution infrastructure and controllable imperfect outcomes; backend implementations and failure mechanisms appear in Appendices E and F.

3.3 Task Construction and Validation

Template-to-scene construction.

Figure 2 summarizes the shared construction pipeline in BEHAVIOR (Srivastava et al., 2021) and ProcTHOR (Deitke et al., 2022; Kolve et al., 2017), which diversify scene styles and layouts. Using template constraints, the constructor matches scenes and binds roles to objects, checking required objects and fixtures against interaction and spatial constraints, using scene profiles in ProcTHOR and scene–template matching with asset materialization in BEHAVIOR. Initialization sets object placements, containment, agent pose, and task-relevant states with synchronized visual representations. For dishware inspection, a dirty item is placed where exploration is needed to discover it; the instruction specifies inspection and handling requirements without revealing the target. Rule-based subtask decomposition guides execution validation. Configuration details appear in Appendix G.

Static and execution validation.

Static checks test role and condition consistency, initial-state reconstruction, nontrivial goals, and reachability. A privileged teacher follows the reference decomposition through Oracle System 1, checking goal satisfaction and configured events; failure-injection instances must recover to completion with failures enabled. Traces and videos support inspection. We construct 870 executable tasks from 35 base templates and their compositions (Appendix G).

Situated QA attachment.

About 3,500 questions from eight QA templates probe object states, spatial relations, action outcomes, anomalies, new requirements, and task progress. Candidates derived from task semantics are screened against teacher traces for valid activation and resolvable answers. Evaluation triggers questions at configured actions, steps, or subtask milestones, with answers determined from the evaluated episode’s corresponding state (Appendix I).

4 SCOPER-harness

Prior embodied systems use environmental feedback and explicit memory to support planning (Huang et al., 2022c; Wang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2022a; Jatavallabhula et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2023). Our evaluations expose two difficulties in closed-loop task execution: maintaining scene evidence to guide task decomposition and subsequent decisions, and detecting unsuccessful execution to support recovery. We introduce SCOPER-harness, a training-free harness that addresses these difficulties through Evidence Memory and Progress Verification. A dynamic agenda connects accumulated evidence to task requirements, while anti-deadlock control balances information gathering with task advancement. All model-based components share the same fixed-parameter backbone through role-specific prompts and use no additional privileged simulator information. Figure 3 summarizes the architecture.

4.1 Evidence Memory and Adaptive Task Decomposition

Structured evidence memory.

Partial observations require retaining evidence without treating missing observations as state changes. We maintain Mt=(Ft,It,Ot)M_{t}=(F_{t},I_{t},O_{t}): facts store object properties, relations, and scene descriptions with evidence and validity annotations; incidents record execution discrepancies and handling status; obligations track outstanding observation or action needs linked to relevant objects and incidents.

Instruction-derived agenda.

The agenda AtA_{t} organizes required outcomes, ongoing constraints, and conditional requirements, while memory obligations track observation or handling needs. Initialization uses only the instruction, retaining unresolved conditions as inspection needs without assuming unseen states or fixing an action sequence. Items track status and supporting evidence.

Observation-driven memory updates.

Before decisions, discovery extracts task-relevant objects and states from current and available execution-process images; reconciliation checks facts against new evidence. Confirmation refreshes evidence, contradiction invalidates facts, and newer scene descriptions can supersede older ones; invisibility alone does not negate a fact. A deterministic commit layer checks references, evidence links, and consistency before committing model updates.

Evidence-grounded agenda revision.

Committed memory drives agenda revision: the model combines the instruction, existing items, and new evidence to activate conditional requirements, add necessary work within task scope, merge duplicates, and update or reopen affected items. Inspection items become supported when the required information is obtained; execution items require verified effects, while ongoing constraints remain monitored. Unresolved inspection needs guide observation actions toward relevant objects or conditions. For example, “inspect the kitchen and turn off any running faucets” initializes inspection and conditional shutoff requirements. Observing running water supports the corresponding state check and activates shutoff work, but does not establish that the faucet has been turned off.

Context Routing and Action Selection.

Deterministic routing selects committed memory within a bounded context, prioritizing relevant facts and unresolved needs while retaining evidence references and validity annotations. The policy receives the routed memory M~t\widetilde{M}_{t} together with the instruction xx, recent images VtV_{t}, public action-request history HtH_{t}, agenda AtA_{t}, and control context ctc_{t}: at=πθ​(x,Vt,Ht,At,M~t,ct)a_{t}=\pi_{\theta}(x,V_{t},H_{t},A_{t},\widetilde{M}_{t},c_{t}). The control context specifies available tools and arguments, the recovery phase, and action restrictions. The policy outputs one tool call with arguments. Request history records issued tool requests but provides no ground-truth success labels.

4.2 Progress Verification and Recovery

Visual verification and recovery feedback.

Issuing an action does not establish progress. Navigation and manipulation therefore receive outcome verification; exploration supplies memory observations without separate verification. Given the tool request, expected state and visual effects, and immediate before-and-after images, the verifier returns success, failure, or ambiguity with visual evidence. Success commits supported effects and resolves satisfied needs; failure records discrepancies and recovery obligations; ambiguity leaves outcomes unconfirmed. Memory adopts the verifier’s effect assessment without readjudicating the same images; later observations may revise it. In the faucet example, stopped flow supports completion; continued flow leaves shutoff unresolved and triggers recovery. The original request, evidence, and recovery state guide further observation, renewed approach, or retry. Verified subsequent effects update memory and the agenda, returning local recovery to task planning.

4.3 Anti-Deadlock Control

Balancing exploration, execution, and recovery budgets.

Evidence maintenance and verification can encourage excessive exploration or conservative checking. The controller tracks scans, searches, and navigation by room/target, and observations and retries per incident. At exploration limits, it restricts tools and requests reselection to promote approach and interaction. The agenda guides planning; recovery and anti-deadlock rules constrain execution. Reselection and recovery are budgeted. Exhaustion terminates execution or permits continuation with unresolved state, depending on the recovery branch. Temporary planning assumptions remain separate from verified facts, cannot support agenda completion, and remain revisable by later evidence. Appendix J details memory and agenda records and states, routing order and capacities, recovery fields and transitions, counter updates and resets, branch rules, prompt responsibilities, and execution pseudocode.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026), Gemini-3.8-flash (Google DeepMind, 2026), Embodied-R1.5 (Yuan et al., 2026), RoboBrain2.5-8B (Tan et al., 2026), RynnBrain11-9B (Li et al., 2026), Molmo2-ER-4B (Fang et al., 2026), Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a), and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b) in ProcTHOR (Deitke et al., 2022) and BEHAVIOR (Srivastava et al., 2021). All eight models follow the shared Oracle System 1 interface and input protocol (Section 3.1), using 512×512512\times 512 RGB observations without privileged simulator state. For Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B, we compare direct execution against the same-backbone, training-free SCOPER-harness (Section 4). Given the limited gains and substantially higher cost of pairing GPT-6-Astra with the harness, we exclude this configuration from the full comparison. Across methods, atomic/two-subtask/three-subtask episodes allow 24/36/48 high-level calls, including QA answers. Tool interfaces, observation processing, and model/harness configurations appear in Appendices A, E, and J; model-call overhead is described in Appendix L.

SR is the task success fraction; Prog./Cov. are task-averaged fractions of satisfied goal predicates/covered required actions. QA (T/A) denotes triggered/configured questions and correctly answered/triggered questions, respectively, counting triggered but unanswered questions as incorrect. Aggregates weight task metrics by task counts and QA metrics by their respective question denominators. Success conditions and detailed scoring rules appear in Appendix A. Additional action-step and blind evaluations appear in Appendices B and C. Figure 4 illustrates why fixed instruction-derived action sequences can be insufficient. Further examples appear in Appendix K.

5.2 Main Results

General-purpose capability matters.

Table 1 shows that GPT-6 Astra leads direct execution with overall SRs of 50.5% on BEHAVIOR and 35.1% on ProcTHOR, versus 14.8% and 21.1% for Qwen3.8-27B. Its necessary-action coverage is higher on both backends; only one of its 500 failed episodes ended in a parsing error. These results suggest strengths in reliable tool use, multi-step progression, observation-grounded action selection, outcome monitoring, and recovery. Embodied-specialized models show no consistent advantage, suggesting that gains on open-loop embodied evaluations need not transfer to closed-loop execution. Nevertheless, 58.6% of Astra’s failures exhausted the action budget, indicating limits in exploration efficiency and recovery planning.

Harness gains across models and backends.

SCOPER-harness raises overall SR by 24.8/28.6 percentage points on BEHAVIOR and 16.9/11.1 on ProcTHOR for Qwen3.5-9B/Qwen3.8-27B, respectively. SR, progress, and necessary-action coverage improve in every task group for both models on both backends. Qwen3.5-9B with SCOPER-harness surpasses direct Qwen3.8-27B execution on both backends. Additional inference calls organizing Evidence Memory, adaptive planning, and recovery thus improve fixed-model performance.

Situated QA complements execution metrics.

GPT-6 Astra leads overall QA trigger rates on both backends while maintaining high accuracy on triggered questions, consistent with its task performance. SCOPER-harness increases trigger rates in all four backbone–backend combinations and triggered accuracy in three. Accuracy must be read alongside trigger rate: execution paths activate different question sets, precluding an identical-question interpretation.

Failure patterns motivate evidence and progress control.

Across the six open-source models’ 4,813 failed normal-image episodes, 47.7% stopped prematurely and 30.7% exhausted the action budget, reflecting difficulties in completion assessment, state tracking, and sustained progress. At least three consecutive identical tool calls occurred in 40.2%, suggesting difficulty adapting unsuccessful strategies; parsing failures accounted for 12.8%, and reference-binding issues appeared in 17.3%. This motivates evidence-based completion checks, state tracking, repetition-aware recovery, and clearer tool/reference conventions. These indicators overlap rather than partition failure causes.

5.3 Harness Component Ablations

Table 2 separately ablates anti-deadlock control, explicit recovery, and Evidence Memory using Qwen3.8-27B on both backends. Each w/o disables only the named component; Recovery denotes Progress Verification and its associated recovery mechanism.

Anti-deadlock control sustains progress.

Removing this component lowers overall SR by 11.8/17.6 percentage points on ProcTHOR/BEHAVIOR, reducing progress and necessary-action coverage in every task group. Trajectories show prolonged exploration and repeated confirmation without physical operations, also seen in direct execution and potentially reinforced by harness evidence and verification. Exploration limits and action commitment prevent budget exhaustion.

Explicit recovery supports anomaly handling.

Without recovery, failure-recovery SR drops from 39.2% to 27.7% on ProcTHOR and 65.4% to 21.5% on BEHAVIOR, while routine execution and observation-dependent performance remain largely stable or improve slightly. This selective decline supports verification and recovery for identifying unmet action effects and organizing corrective actions, with benefits concentrated in anomaly handling.

Memory supports observation-dependent decisions.

Removing Evidence Memory lowers observation-dependent SR from 37.8% to 33.3% on ProcTHOR and from 34.4% to 17.8% on BEHAVIOR. Composite SR also falls from 30.0% to 23.0% on BEHAVIOR, with a smaller change on ProcTHOR. This supports retaining evidence for subsequent observation-dependent decisions.

5.4 Real-Observation Evaluation

We test transfer of simulation findings through offline next-tool-call evaluation on 200 distinct AgiBotWorld2026 (AgiBot, 2026) demonstration episodes: 80 normal-execution, 60 observation-dependent, and 60 involving anomalous or incomplete actions and repair. At each node, direct execution and SCOPER-harness predict the next tool call from the instruction, current semantic action segment’s head-camera images, and preceding reference actions; predictions are not propagated as executed actions. We report tool accuracy and full-call accuracy (correct tool and all required arguments), separately evaluating observation-critical and repair-decision nodes. This fixed-history evaluation tests real-visual decisions, but not active observation acquisition, consequences of agents’ own errors, or sustained multi-step recovery. It complements closed-loop simulation testing task completion through continued interaction. Construction and scoring appear in Appendix D. Consistent with simulation (Table 3), GPT-6 Astra leads overall full-call accuracy at 70.8%, while embodied-specialized models show no consistent advantage. SCOPER-harness raises full-call accuracy from 33.9% to 48.6% for Qwen3.5-9B and 44.3% to 59.6% for Qwen3.8-27B. Observation-critical call accuracy improves by 26.7/27.8 percentage points, respectively, and repair-call accuracy by 28.4 points for both, benefiting real visual decisions, especially critical nodes.

6 Conclusion

We introduced the SCOPER suite for studying embodied System 2 through closed-loop, observation-grounded planning and recovery. SCOPER-bench combines high-level goals, execution-time observations, and controlled failures in 870 tasks across two simulators. SCOPER-harness connects accumulated scene evidence and verified action outcomes to an evolving task agenda, improving performance across the evaluated models and on real-observation decision tests. These findings highlight the importance of using observations to determine required work and revise decisions throughout execution. Future work will extend the current skill interface toward richer, more continuous action spaces and broader action coverage, and adapt the benchmark and harness to more complex scenes with greater diversity, dynamics, and interaction demands.

AI use statement

We used Codex and the models GPT-5.6-Sol, GPT-6-Astra, and Gemini-3.8-flash for AI-assisted research discussions and code implementation. AI assistance also supported manuscript drafting and revision, literature search and reference checking, and figure-script editing. The benchmark additionally uses AI models as evaluated agents, as described in the experimental setup. The authors directed these uses, reviewed and revised the assisted content, and take responsibility for the final paper and its scientific claims.

Reproducibility statement

Section 3 describes benchmark construction and evaluation, and Section 4 presents the harness. The appendices document task templates and dataset statistics (Appendix G), execution infrastructure and controlled failures (Appendices E and F), evaluation protocols and situated QA (Appendices A and I), and harness state definitions and pseudocode (Appendix J). Real-observation evaluation details are provided in Appendix D. Additional supporting files will be provided as supplementary material.
