Appendix A Evaluation Protocol

Evaluation compares closed-loop execution through a shared skill interface and task-level scorer. This section specifies episode interaction, available information, and aggregation; detailed QA definitions appear in Appendix I.

A.1 Interaction, Observations, and Information Access

Each episode loads a task, initializes the scene and event schedulers, and produces initial RGB images. The model emits one skill request from its current decision context; Binding resolves public references, System 1 executes admitted requests, and the interface supplies images and request records for the next decision. A separate evaluator checks goals and events.

All evaluated methods receive public instructions, tool definitions, RGB images, and permitted request records. Simulator inventories and identifiers, role mappings, ground-truth states and poses, distances, goal progress, injection labels, teacher trajectories, and reference decompositions remain internal. Public vocabulary defines valid references rather than scene contents. Harness memory, agenda, and visual assessments derive from public inputs. Execution-admission signals are used by the deterministic controller only for gating and budget accounting; executor success flags and diagnostic records are excluded from model inputs.

Navigation, scanning, and target search each produce up to eight process-observation frames, retaining the current view; ordinary manipulation supplies before-and-after RGB images. These observations enter a visual history maintained across actions. Direct evaluation models receive the latest available frames, up to 32, together with public action-request history at each decision. The harness uniformly samples up to eight frames from navigation, scanning, and search for observation maintenance; its policy uses up to the latest four frames, public request history, and routed memory. Since memory retains evidence from earlier observations, the policy uses fewer recent frames than direct evaluation. When fewer frames are available, all available frames within the respective limit are used. Instructions, public vocabulary, and tool definitions remain accessible throughout execution.

The harness uses Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B; policy, verification, memory, and agenda calls within an experiment use the same fixed-parameter base model. Additional model calls contribute computational cost rather than additional environmental observations; acquiring a different viewpoint or position requires a public tool request and consumes the corresponding interaction budget.

Direct-model evaluation uses an input image resolution of 512×512512\times 512; GPT-6 uses the max reasoning-effort setting.

A.2 Evaluation Prompts and Per-Decision Context

The fixed system prompt assigns the model the role of an embodied agent completing the task with the listed skills. It supplies the instruction, tool names and argument definitions, public reference rules, and general action prerequisites. Instructions specify objectives, scope, and conditional requirements. Shared guidance covers approaching objects before interaction, assessing effects from images, observing again when needed, and stopping after all task clauses are satisfied; the model chooses the task-specific action sequence.

Each user turn contains the current step, remaining tool budget, the previous requested skill and public arguments, chronologically ordered action-request history, and the current image input. The request-history limit follows the episode’s high-level budget, capped at 48 entries, allowing preceding requests to be retained within the prescribed 24-, 36-, or 48-step episodes. Each entry states what was requested without an action-success label. Full user–assistant conversations are not replayed by default, and old images are not repeatedly embedded in the history text; previously generated reasoning is not retained as permanent environmental evidence.

The model outputs one tool name and its arguments, optionally accompanied by a short rationale. The interface parses the request before Binding and execution. The next-turn summary repeats the requested call and states that it has finished; the model assesses its outcome from images.

The following layout distinguishes fixed interaction rules from turn-specific content. Images are attached chronologically as image inputs; dynamic content comes from the public task and interaction records. New task messages enter subsequent task context, whereas QA messages use a dedicated answer format.

System: Complete the task using the available tools. Task: [instruction and public task updates]. Tools: [names and argument definitions]. Follow the public reference rules and interaction prerequisites. Use images to assess outcomes; a requested action does not establish success. Return one tool call with arguments.

Decision turn: Step: [current step]. Remaining budget: [remaining calls]. Previous requests: [public action history]. Last request: [tool and arguments; call finished]. Visual input: [ordered frames]. Choose the next call.

QA turn: Question: [identifier, text, and choices]. Use the permitted current context and return the question identifier and selected answer value.

When a situated question is posted, a separate answer call supplies its public identifier, text, choices, and the visual and execution context permitted at that time; the model responds with the question identifier and selected answer value. Newly introduced task requirements are supplied as public natural-language messages and distinguished from questions requesting only an answer. After stopping, the prompt specifies an answer-only phase without further physical actions; goal checking and answer correctness remain evaluator-side operations.

A.3 Budgets and Termination

Atomic, two-subtask, and three-subtask episodes use high-level call budgets of 24, 36, and 48, respectively, shared across compared methods. Observation, manipulation, answering, and stopping are counted under a common protocol; appended QA answers also consume this budget. Internal verification, memory maintenance, and action reselection calls are recorded separately, enabling separate comparisons of environment-interaction efficiency and model-call cost.

Under the standard stop-and-QA finishing protocol, stop ends physical execution and freezes its task score. Pending questions are handled in an answer-only finishing phase using the remaining budget, without resuming physical actions. Physical completion and subsequent answers can therefore be scored separately.

Task completion is determined from environment state at scoring time and applicable process conditions, rather than a model’s completion claim or earlier goal attainment. Let 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} denote an episode’s goal predicates. We set si=1s_{i}=1 exactly when all predicates hold and the task’s configured stopping requirement is satisfied. A stop call freezes the goal score; if the budget expires without stopping, the last available state is evaluated and any unmet stopping requirement remains unsatisfied. Budget exhaustion is additionally recorded as a runner failure, so runner status and physical task success are reported separately.

For composite tasks, handoff records local child completion, whereas overall scoring uses the parent task’s required goal set; handoff records do not replace the overall goal check. Event records separately establish whether an intervention was triggered and applied. An untriggered intervention provides no evidence of successful recovery. Goal scores, intervention application, and QA scores remain distinct.

A.4 Metrics and Aggregation

We compute task metrics over a common set 𝒟\mathcal{D} of scored episodes, including both successful tasks and agent failures during valid evaluation. Infrastructure errors and unfinished runs are recorded separately rather than counted as task successes or failures. Task-group and template results use the corresponding subsets; proportions below are reported as percentages.

Success Rate (SR).

SR measures the fraction of episodes satisfying their final success conditions:

SR=1|𝒟|​∑i∈𝒟si,si∈{0,1}.\mathrm{SR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}s_{i},\qquad s_{i}\in\{0,1\}. (1)

Here, sis_{i} is the evaluator’s task_success indicator, requiring the scored state to satisfy the task goals, including applicable process conditions, and stopping conditions. It is neither the model’s completion claim nor merely a successful runner termination.

Task Progress (Prog.).

Progress measures partial completion. Let 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} be the goal predicates of episode ii and gi​j∈{0,1}g_{ij}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether predicate jj holds at scoring time. We first compute the satisfied fraction within each episode and then average over episodes:

Prog.=1|𝒟|​∑i∈𝒟∑j∈𝒢igi​j|𝒢i|.\mathrm{Prog.}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{G}_{i}}g_{ij}}{|\mathcal{G}_{i}|}. (2)

Thus, tasks with more predicates do not automatically receive greater weight.

Goal items can be environmental predicates or evaluator-recorded process conditions. Container inspection uses two goal items: a valid interior inspection and the condition-dependent final openness. Logical branches of that condition are not separate scoring items.

Necessary Action Coverage (Cov.).

Coverage measures how many required actions from the teacher policy’s reference execution are covered. For each task, a validated teacher trajectory is compiled into a deduplicated reference action set with dependency constraints ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i}, which serves as the ground-truth reference for this metric. Matching uses the normalized tool, the resolved execution target, and the manipulated object for placement or release. Same-object causal dependencies and composite-stage constraints are retained, while unrelated actions may be reordered. Only execution-confirmed matches count; matching request names or repeated attempts alone do not increase coverage. References remain private to the evaluator.

Let 𝒞i⊆ℛi\mathcal{C}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{i} contain the matched reference actions. Coverage is normalized within each task before averaging:

Cov.=1|𝒟|​∑i∈𝒟|𝒞i||ℛi|.\mathrm{Cov.}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}\frac{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|}{|\mathcal{R}_{i}|}. (3)

This measures execution coverage relative to the teacher reference, rather than shortest-path efficiency or final goal correctness, and is reported separately from SR and progress.

QA aggregation includes only questions with valid evaluator answer keys. Questions whose keys cannot be resolved are recorded separately and excluded from the corresponding configured and posted counts, as well as correct-answer counts. Missing, incorrect, or unparseable model responses are not answer-key resolution failures and remain incorrect responses to valid posted questions.

QA Trigger Rate and Triggered QA Accuracy (T / A).

These metrics distinguish reaching question checkpoints from answering them correctly. Let qiq_{i}, pip_{i}, and cic_{i} denote the numbers of valid configured, valid posted, and correctly answered situated questions in episode ii. The main tables report

T=∑i∈𝒟pi∑i∈𝒟qi,A=∑i∈𝒟ci∑i∈𝒟pi.T=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}p_{i}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}q_{i}},\qquad A=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}c_{i}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}p_{i}}. (4)

Questions eligible for activation but still awaiting delivery in the queue do not count as posted.

Triggered but unanswered questions count as incorrect in AA; untriggered questions are excluded from its denominator but reduce TT. A metric with a zero denominator is reported as unavailable. Different execution paths can expose different question sets, so accuracy is interpreted alongside trigger rate. These metrics concern situated QA.

Average Steps.

Let LiL_{i} be the number of high-level calls counted by the interaction protocol in episode ii. We report

AvgSteps=1|𝒟|​∑i∈𝒟Li.\mathrm{AvgSteps}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}L_{i}. (5)

Both successful and failed episodes are included. Observation, navigation, manipulation, answering, and stopping follow the shared counting protocol; low-level simulator actions and internal harness model calls are excluded. Atomic, two-subtask, and three-subtask budgets are 24, 36, and 48 calls, respectively. Fewer steps can result from early failure, so this metric is not designated lower-is-better.

Aggregation.

SR, progress, coverage, and average steps are weighted by episode counts; QA metrics are weighted by their respective question denominators. We do not directly average template or category percentages or assign equal weight to per-episode QA accuracies. Overall results are computed from underlying counts or equivalent denominator-weighted aggregates.

Appendix B High-Level Action Counts

Table 4 reports average high-level calls; these should be interpreted jointly with task completion. On ProcTHOR, RoboBrain2.5-8B uses 10.08 steps with 5.8% success, whereas Qwen3.8-27B uses 20.68 steps and achieves 21.1% success. Shorter trajectories therefore do not necessarily imply more effective execution.

Appendix C Blind Evaluation

To verify that SCOPER-bench requires visual observations rather than textual shortcuts, we replace all visual inputs with black images. Tables 5 and 6 report the results for BEHAVIOR and ProcTHOR, respectively. All models exhibit near-zero task completion, relying largely on prior-based guesses. These results demonstrate that the benchmark requires visual perception and cannot be solved through simple instruction decomposition.

Appendix D Real-Robot Next-Tool-Call Evaluation

D.1 Data and Decision-Node Construction

The evaluation uses real-robot demonstrations from AgiBotWorld2026, excluding simulation data. The 200 distinct source episodes form three mutually exclusive groups: 80 normal-execution, 60 observation-dependent, and 60 involving anomalous or incomplete actions and their repair. Each sample covers a contiguous task scope with a defined objective and termination condition within one source video; videos are not spliced together. An episode can yield multiple decision nodes, so episode counts differ from scored-decision counts.

Videos are segmented into semantic actions such as navigation, picking, placing, and opening or closing containers. Local camera, torso, and gripper adjustments are generally absorbed into their semantic segment, whereas necessary base approaches are represented as navigation. For reference calls (a1,…,aK)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{K}), the node after segment ii receives the reference prefix through aia_{i} and targets ai+1a_{i+1}; the final segment is followed by finish(). Scoring begins after the first segment and does not predict the initial action. Every node uses reference history rather than predictions from preceding nodes.

D.2 Observations and Challenge Categories

Visual inputs use the head-camera stream observation.images.top_head, sampled at 0.5 FPS on a fixed temporal grid anchored at the start of the selected task scope. Each node receives only grid frames within the current segment and no later than its endpoint, without accumulating raw images from earlier segments. Textual action history retains the complete reference prefix. Future frames, manually selected keyframes, bounding-box annotations, success or failure labels, category labels, and reference answers are withheld.

English instructions are reconstructed from source annotations and videos, specifying execution order where necessary. Observation-dependent instructions describe inspection requirements without revealing the object or state to discover; repair instructions do not identify a failed action. Each observation-dependent episode includes at least one node whose next call requires current visual evidence. Nodes requiring future images to resolve ambiguity are excluded from scoring.

Recovery samples include naturally occurring anomalies with verifiable subsequent recovery and incomplete-action nodes constructed by splitting an original action before completion. For example, a pickup segment can be divided into an unfinished pickup and its continuation, followed by placement. The latter preserves the original images but does not imply an actual grasp failure or controller retry. The two sources are labeled separately, and decisions that resume the task after repair are evaluated.

D.3 Harness State Along Reference Execution

The harness maintains memory and the agenda along the reference execution prefix. The initial agenda is derived from the instruction, and state is updated using images and reference calls provided up to the current node. Raw image input still covers only the current segment; earlier observations can persist through memory. Predicted calls are not executed, do not enter reference history, and do not authorize committing expected effects. Subsequent updates follow the reference video and actions without future frames or answer labels.

D.4 Output Interface and Metrics

Each node freely generates one structured call without candidate options or a complete future plan. Tools include navigate_to, pick, place, open/close, turn_on/turn_off, soak_under, and finish, with data-dependent extensions fixed before evaluation. Object arguments are matched at category level using a frozen alias mapping; instance identifiers, colors, coordinates, and hand selection are not evaluated. Placement specifies the destination without repeating the held object’s category. The interface contains no inspect tool.

Tool Accuracy measures the fraction of nodes with the correct tool name. The primary metric, Call Accuracy, requires the tool and all necessary arguments to match one complete reference. Argument errors invalidate the call but not a correct tool name; unparseable outputs or unknown tools fail both metrics. The argument-free finish() receives identical judgments. Equivalent references must be matched as complete calls rather than by combining their components.

Category and overall results are aggregated over decision nodes; overall accuracy divides total correct predictions by all scorable nodes. Observation-critical Call Accuracy and Repair-decision Call Accuracy use their respective subsets without adding them again to the overall denominator. Post-repair continuation nodes contribute to the repair category. Because predictions do not control the robot or subsequent observations, this evaluation reports no task success, goal progress, action coverage, or average execution steps.

Appendix E Oracle System 1 and Teacher Policy

Oracle System 1 is skill-execution infrastructure shared by evaluated models and the teacher. It implements individual skill requests through rules; the teacher policy reads the task specification and selects skill sequences for reference execution and validation. We describe skill execution and teacher organization separately below.

E.1 Unified Skill Abstraction

System 1 converts high-level requests into controlled scene changes and provides visual observations of their execution and outcomes. Table 7 summarizes skills by shared semantics: navigation and observation establish information and interaction poses, while manipulation updates object poses, relations, or properties. Object-state processing can be realized by a dedicated skill or a composition of existing skills.

E.2 Tool Arguments and Model-Facing Outputs

Table 8 summarizes model-facing tool arguments. Unless noted otherwise, listed arguments are required strings; object_ref uses a public concrete category or supported alias rather than a private role or object identifier. Skills share semantics, with interface differences stated only where necessary: ProcTHOR includes room navigation in navigate_to, whereas BEHAVIOR additionally exposes room navigation and several state-processing tools. Models receive only the tool definitions available in the current backend.

Wiping, washing under a source, filling, pouring, and dedicated heating and cooling tools are exposed by BEHAVIOR; corresponding ProcTHOR state effects arise through the container, device, and placement operations described above. State transitions occur inside System 1, while the model receives prescribed execution images and a request-completion summary, not state values, held-object inventories, ground-truth spatial relations, or effect labels. Answering and stopping are protocol operations and do not acquire additional scene information.

E.3 Navigation and Observation Implementation

Navigation constructs its search space from scene collision and reachability information and uses A* to reach an interaction pose near the target. ProcTHOR searches a grid of reachable positions and executes movement and rotation along the path. BEHAVIOR searches an occupancy grid accounting for the agent footprint and validates connectivity and path feasibility; its eight-connected search disallows diagonal corner cutting through blocked cells.

Navigation, scanning, and target search provide images during execution through backend observation callbacks. Scanning covers surrounding views, while target search organizes target-directed observation. The evaluation interface selects and delivers observations to the model or harness, connecting scene discovery to action selection throughout execution.

E.4 Manipulation and State Synchronization

Manipulation controls poses, attachment relations, and object properties through rules, bypassing low-level grasp and contact dynamics. ProcTHOR’s controlled pickup and placement maintain visual attachment and containment relations alongside simulator state operations. BEHAVIOR’s symbolic executor updates held states, spatial relations, and properties and synchronizes these changes with rendered objects and joints. Both retain object-affordance, access, and interaction preconditions.

State processing follows the semantics of the corresponding operation. For example, ProcTHOR implements cleaning through sink and faucet interactions and cooling or heating through container and device operations. BEHAVIOR uses corresponding state operations and execution wrappers for cleaning, cutting, and temperature changes. A shared capability therefore need not correspond to an identically named standalone tool on both backends. The resulting scene and images provide evidence for subsequent outcome checking.

Manipulation skills use controlled state transitions that bypass low-level motion and contact simulation while retaining immediate pre- and post-action RGB observations for outcome checking. Navigation and exploration additionally provide multi-frame process observations, allowing the model to discover objects and conditions during execution.

The teacher policy uses task specifications and environment truth to organize skill calls into reference trajectories. Routine strategies satisfy goal predicates, observation-dependent strategies handle scene issues to be discovered, recovery strategies address execution deviations, and composite strategies coordinate subtasks. Reference trajectories support feasibility, goal, and event validation and provide execution context for QA attachment. Evaluated models execute through the same System 1 skill interface.

Appendix F Controlled Failure Injection and Scene Disturbances

Controlled interventions turn routine skill execution into closed-loop tasks requiring monitoring and recovery. We distinguish execution failures that alter the current skill’s outcome from scene disturbances that change the environment after an execution milestone. Both are specified by activation conditions and state transformations in the task configuration, allowing the same task goal to be paired with different recovery challenges.

F.1 Activation and Scheduling

We represent an event as e=(τ,r,h,ϕ,n)e=(\tau,r,h,\phi,n), where τ\tau specifies an eligible skill or milestone, rr identifies the target role, hh defines activation conditions, ϕ\phi specifies the state intervention, and nn bounds the number of firings. Conditions can depend on a particular action result, elapsed action steps, containment or non-held states, and the owning subtask being active. Configurations also support probabilities and cooldown intervals to control intervention frequency.

Execution failures intercept a matching skill call or modify its outcome, whereas scene disturbances check conditions and apply changes after the relevant execution milestone. The scheduler maintains event histories and firing counts and scopes events to their owning subtask. Eligibility and whether the intended state change was actually applied are recorded separately for task validation.

F.2 Failure Mechanisms

Table 9 summarizes six concrete failure mechanisms. They alter holding, placement, openness, or navigation outcomes, requiring subsequent actions to be revised from actual observations. For example, a dropped placement releases the object outside its destination; recovery requires localization and pickup before another placement attempt.

Object release and relocation use controlled pose and held-relation updates and refresh subsequent observations. Dropped placement selects a location outside the destination; BEHAVIOR additionally checks collision, reachability, and rendered visibility and restores the prior state if the relocation cannot be committed. Partial opening and closing modify openness and its visual configuration. Wrong-target navigation substitutes the executed target while retaining the original request for outcome checking.

Incomplete navigation simulates failure to arrive by modifying the final pose. ProcTHOR repositions the agent to an intermediate location between the start and endpoint after nominal navigation; BEHAVIOR selects a pre-terminal pose from the planned route. This mechanism creates an outcome requiring further navigation without adding a physical obstacle to the scene.

F.3 State-Changing Disturbances

Scene disturbances can reclose or reopen containers, toggle devices, re-dirty objects, and relocate or restore objects. Activation connects these changes to meaningful task stages: for example, moving a staged object once it is no longer held, or re-dirtying an object after cleaning and intervening actions. Such events require the model to revisit previously valid facts and restore disrupted prerequisites or goals.

Both backends implement disturbances through scene-state changes and synchronize the visual representation of object poses, joints, or properties. Task validation checks final goals together with required interventions, ensuring that reference trajectories encounter the intended challenge. The evaluator retains private event records, while models assess consequences from protocol-provided observations and public interaction information.

Appendix G Task Templates and Construction

Templates translate capability requirements into instantiable object, state, and event constraints. We organize tasks into Routine Execution, Observation-dependent, Failure Recovery, and Composite. Below we describe shared template fields, instantiation, and representative instances. Tables below summarize each benchmark template through its roles, initialization requirements, and goal predicates.

G.1 Dataset Statistics and Scene Sampling

The construction target is ten task instances per base template in each simulator, together with 50 two-child and 50 three-child composite tasks per simulator. The 35 base templates thus yield a target of 450 tasks per backend. Limited matches across diverse BEHAVIOR scenes lead to the exclusion of 30 instances, leaving 420 BEHAVIOR and 450 ProcTHOR tasks, or 870 tasks in total. ProcTHOR contains 130 routine-execution, 90 observation-dependent, 130 failure-recovery, and 100 composite episodes. BEHAVIOR contains 100, 90, 130, and 100 episodes in the corresponding groups, with the 30 excluded instances belonging to routine execution. ProcTHOR scenes are randomly sampled from its official pool of 12,000 scenes. For BEHAVIOR, filtering out excessively large scenes leaves a pool of 35 distinct scenes for task matching; task objects are randomly added under the template’s compatibility constraints.

G.2 Template Specification and Instantiation

Each template specifies object roles, categories or category groups, affordance requirements, and relations between roles. Initial conditions describe open/closed, cleanliness, containment, or location states, and goal predicates define the desired outcome. Instruction patterns replace roles with public object descriptions; event configurations define challenge triggers and consequences; composite tasks additionally retain subtask identities and scopes.

Scene matching first filters candidates by object type and affordance, then checks same-room, cross-room, distinctness, and spatial constraints. ProcTHOR profiles provide object and scene information. The BEHAVIOR matcher can reuse the shared JSON templates and distinguishes direct matches, matches requiring spawned assets, and matches requiring runtime validation. Bound tasks satisfy initial conditions through permitted relocation, state configuration, or asset materialization.

Initialization applies these configurations to concrete objects and synchronizes rendered state. Validation checks initial predicates, geometry and support relations, navigation and sequential interaction reachability, and whether all goals already hold. Teacher rollouts then check final goals and required events. Scenes unable to support a template retain explicit rejection reasons.

Instructions specify task objectives, scope, and handling rules without exposing construction-time instance bindings or step-by-step procedures. In observation-conditioned tasks, the model identifies the concrete objects requiring attention and their current states from scene observations. Public category terms express selection criteria rather than enumerate qualifying scene instances. The model consequently determines action targets, necessary prerequisites, and subsequent operations.

For tasks with universal inspection requirements, construction ensures that all actionable issues within the instruction scope are represented in template bindings and scoring goals; other relevant objects are initialized in compliant states. Instructions such as switching everything off or closing all containers therefore introduce no additional initial issues outside the scoring scope.

For example, clean-dishware storage requires dishware, storage, and distinguishable dirty-dishware distractors. The matcher selects instances satisfying affordance and spatial constraints; initialization makes target dishware clean, makes distractor dishware dirty, and configures placement under the template constraints. The public instruction requests storing clean dishware and excluding dirty dishware from storage, without identifying which concrete instances belong to either group or prescribing a pickup-and-placement sequence. Final goals jointly require target storage, exclusion of distractors from storage, and container closure where applicable.

G.3 Representative Templates

Routine execution includes simple placement and preparation before storage. Simple placement transfers a pickupable object to a destination; preparation requires cleaning, cutting, heating, or cooling before the placement goal. Multi-stage preparation combines these requirements into an object workflow.

The dirty-dish workflow template includes dishware, sink, faucet, and storage roles and can include a staging surface. The dish is initialized dirty and outside storage, and the goal requires it to be clean and stored. The task connects identifying issues in the scene to subsequent cleaning and storage, making observations determine which objects and operations require attention.

Safety inspection initializes a running faucet and an open container in one room and requires both to be closed or switched off. Other observation templates include cross-room inspection, mixed issues, and category-dependent storage. Latent issue records specify the actual initial conditions and required handling, while the model identifies actionable conditions from visual observations.

The dropped-placement template binds a pickupable object and destination, with a goal of establishing the correct placement relation. A one-shot placement event releases the object beside the target, requiring recovery through approach, pickup, and return to the destination. Partial opening or closing, grasp slips, and incorrect navigation alter other execution effects, requiring different recovery procedures toward the same final goal.

Composite tasks contain two or three subtasks and retain each child’s roles, goals, events, and identity. Runtime scheduling scopes events to their owning subtask and advances the active child at handoff. Handoffs are managed by the evaluation process rather than requested by the model. QA can cover different children and handoff progress; overall and per-subtask success are recorded separately.

G.4 Template Structure and Predicate Catalog

Table 10 summarizes template structure. Table 11 describes the 35 benchmark task templates individually through object roles, initialization or event requirements, and goal predicates. Roles satisfy the affordance and access constraints of their operations; the tables highlight spatial conditions that distinguish task semantics.

For a unified notation, P⁡(x,r)P(x,r) denotes the placement relation required by a template, instantiated as containment or surface support; P⁡(X,r)P(X,r) requires the relation for every target in the set. ⋀d∈D¬P⁡(d,r)\bigwedge_{d\in D}\neg P(d,r) requires each distractor to remain outside the destination. C∗​(r)C^{*}(r) requires closure only when the destination is openable. Optional roles contribute goals when instantiated. Event requirements define the challenge alongside initial states but activate during execution.

The benchmark uses 35 task templates. Routine Execution, Observation-dependent, Failure Recovery, and Composite are capability-level groups, and an individual template can involve several capabilities. Initially running faucets or dirty dishes are issues to discover through observation, whereas execution-failure templates alter outcomes during skill calls. Composite tasks are formed by composing the selected templates.

Here, H0​(c)H_{0}(c) records whether dishware is present in the container at initialization; moving contents during execution does not change the branch. Inspected⁡(c)\mathrm{Inspected}(c) records acquisition of an interior observation sufficient to assess the contents, rather than merely requesting an observation tool. Construction validation requires visually discriminable evidence for both presence and absence; an occluded view does not establish inspection. The evaluator records whether an interior view delivered through the public observation interface satisfies the task’s visual inspection condition; invoking a tool without obtaining such a view does not satisfy it. This template permits initial openness to satisfy the state requirement, but the inspection condition is initially unmet, so the complete task still requires execution. This prevents initial openness from determining the correct branch.

G.5 Programmatic Instantiation and Composition

The five observation-conditioned inspection and workflow templates instantiate scene issues through programmatic recipes. Cross-room inspection configures one faucet or container issue in each of two rooms; safety inspection configures faucet and container issues in one room; mixed inspection configures faucet, container, and dirty-dish issues in one room. The dirty-dish workflow recipe configures one dish issue, and the storage-policy recipe configures one misplaced object. Each issue expands into concrete roles, initial states, and handling goals.

The general long-horizon constructor combines two or three subtasks while retaining their roles, events, and goal ownership. Compatible object and state requirements allow the children to share an episode while preserving their individual task specifications. The overall goal collects the required child outcomes, while events and QA are scheduled within child scopes.

G.6 Task Instructions and Execution Mechanisms

Table 12 pairs representative public instructions with categories and execution mechanisms for 35 templates: 13 routine, nine observation-dependent, and 13 recovery templates. Conditional container inspection belongs to the observation-dependent group. Composite tasks combine atomic templates and are not counted again as atomic entries.

Categories follow the same template-family grouping as the result tables, rather than mutually exclusive capability requirements. For example, routine clean-dishware selection still requires visual judgment; device activation and placement with an added instruction belong to the observation-dependent group. Failure Recovery includes four recover_* templates that address initially present anomalies, six skill-outcome failure mechanisms, and three mid-execution disturbances. The mechanism column describes construction settings and is not additional model input.

Object names illustrate possible scene instantiations, and instructions are semantic examples rather than verbatim evaluation prompts. Event triggers and parameters remain task-specific; an intervention is not implied for an entry without a listed disturbance. Situated QA can be attached separately without changing the underlying category.

Composite tasks preserve child goals and event scopes and can combine routine, observation-dependent, and recovery requirements.

Appendix H Binding Procedure

Binding connects action requests expressed in public vocabulary to instance-level System 1 execution. It comprises construction-time role binding and runtime reference resolution: the former determines the task’s concrete scene instances, while the latter converts the model’s selected skill and object reference into an executable request. Both backends use shared resolution semantics and maintain simulator-instance mappings inside their adapters.

H.1 Construction-Time Binding and Public References

During construction, template roles are bound to scene objects according to category, affordance, and spatial constraints. The internal mapping supports initialization, event scheduling, goal scoring, and runtime instance resolution. The model uses instructions and observations to select public object categories and operations, which the infrastructure resolves to concrete instances.

Tool instructions require object arguments to use a complete category name or an explicitly listed alias from the public vocabulary; room navigation uses public room labels from the instruction. Private roles, raw object identifiers, and invented color, position, or state modifiers are not valid references. Broad task concepts such as dishware or storage must be translated through observation into concrete categories supported by the interface.

H.2 Runtime Resolution and Interaction Readiness

At runtime, the resolver normalizes the public reference and filters candidates according to reference-admission rules. Resolution first considers compatible recent interaction focus and task-designated instances, followed by public aliases, activated observation or memory candidates, and permitted scene or room references. Internal task mappings can therefore participate in instance selection among objects of the same category: a task- or subtask-designated object can take precedence over background objects. The model selects the public object category and skill, and the infrastructure resolves the instance. Ambiguity that the applicable rules cannot resolve remains unresolved rather than selecting an arbitrary object.

Reference admission and interaction readiness are checked separately. By default, a model may attempt a public concrete category before seeing the object; candidates requiring observation evidence remain subject to their activation conditions. A valid name consequently guarantees neither existence, localization, nor readiness for manipulation. Interaction additionally requires approaching the target and satisfying affordance and access preconditions. After an object moves or drops, preserving its internal identity does not establish that the previous interaction pose remains valid.

For example, an instruction publicly specifies a drawer while other drawers are present in the scene. When the model requests navigation to drawer, the resolver can identify the corresponding drawer through the task mapping; a subsequent opening request using the same public name can retain the recent interaction focus. The model neither needs nor receives the drawer’s simulator identifier, but must still select the opening operation and determine from returned images whether the drawer opened sufficiently. Likewise, when an instruction requires handling only dirty dishware, category resolution does not tell the model whether the dishware is dirty or replace its observation-based decision to wash it.

H.3 Execution Results and the Model Information Boundary

After reference resolution, the executor checks interaction preconditions and executes admitted skills. Unresolved or rejected requests retain their status for internal accounting. The model-facing summary contains the requested skill and public arguments and states that the call has finished; images provide evidence of the outcome. Binding diagnostics and instance mappings follow the information-access rules in Appendix A.

System 1 provides instance-level execution support; System 2 selects actions, interprets scene observations, and assesses outcomes under the shared evaluation protocol.

Appendix I Situated QA

Situated QA turns understanding of execution state into explicit questions and scores. Questions are generated from template semantics and reference traces, while their actual answers are resolved in the evaluated episode. We describe question types, activation, and scoring below.

I.1 Question Types and Construction

The eight QA templates in Table 13 cover object states and spatial relations, action outcomes, active issues, new obligations, remaining requirements, and composite progress. For example, “Is the bowl now in the cabinet?” probes a relation, “What was the outcome of the placement?” probes an effect, and “Which requirements remain incomplete?” probes progress. Answers use the discrete choices associated with each question type.

All eight question types are generated in a unified pipeline from task semantics, goal predicates, and reference execution traces. Candidate questions are associated with public actions, task milestones, or other configured activation conditions and checked for uniquely resolvable answers. Selection considers diversity of question and action types and subtask coverage in composite tasks, with up to six questions per atomic episode. Scheduler replay validates activation before the selected questions are stored in a separate QA specification.

Questions use public task vocabulary without exposing private instance bindings or answer keys. Action-anchored activation matches the tool and object role, avoiding step-offset mismatches introduced by intervening answers. Answer keys are resolved from the actual evaluated episode under the snapshot rules below, rather than copied from reference traces. All eight QA types use a single selected answer from two to four choices.

The three progress-related templates use different scopes. Remaining-requirement questions ask which listed requirements remain unmet at a stopping milestone, for example, whether cleaning or storage remains incomplete. Mid-execution progress questions ask whether one or two specified requirements hold at an intermediate point, such as whether a bowl is clean and stored, with choices such as both, only the first, only the second, or neither. Composite-progress questions ask which subtask is active after a handoff, with choices identifying a child or indicating that all children are complete.

Each posted question is answered by the same task-executing model in a separate answer-only call. This call uses the currently available public execution context and performs no additional exploration or manipulation. QA therefore measures understanding of acquired information and is scored separately from physical task completion.

I.2 Activation, Queuing, and Answer Time

Activation types include a specified tool result, a task-action step threshold, subtask handoff, a new human instruction, and a stop milestone. Each question fires at most once; child-specific questions activate only within their owning subtask. Multiple eligible questions enter a queue, and the next question is posted only when no previous question remains pending.

Action-outcome questions snapshot the evaluator state of the triggering action; delayed questions identify the original action step. State, relation, and intermediate-progress questions resolve and freeze their answer when posted, so later actions do not change their scoring reference. Resolution failures are recorded separately. Public questions contain the question, choices, and identifier; answer keys remain with the evaluator.

I.3 Scoring

Situated QA uses the trigger rate and triggered accuracy in Appendix A.4: valid posted questions divided by valid configured questions, and correct answers divided by valid posted questions. Posted but unanswered questions count as incorrect; unposted questions are excluded from accuracy, and queued questions are not counted as posted.

Correctness uses exact matching between normalized responses and evaluator-held answer keys. Questions with unresolved answer keys are excluded as invalid and reported separately; missing or unparseable responses to valid posted questions remain incorrect. The main tables report situated QA. Because execution paths may trigger different question sets, accuracy is interpreted together with trigger rate.

Appendix J Harness Details

SCOPER uses role-specific calls to the same fixed-parameter model for observation interpretation, agenda revision, action selection, and effect verification. Deterministic code handles structural and reference checks, memory routing, and bounded execution control. The following specification uses the same state definitions and information flow as the main text.

J.1 Component Inputs and Outputs

Initialization produces an agenda from the task instruction without images. Observation calls receive the instruction, memory to maintain, and available images, and propose evidence-linked updates. Agenda revision receives the instruction, existing items, and committed memory, and proposes additions and modifications. The policy receives the instruction, the latest four frames, up to the latest 48 public tool-request records, routed memory, the agenda, allowed tools and argument definitions, and recovery and anti-deadlock context, and outputs one structured tool call. Procedural guidance is supplied through item-level next intents and public tool descriptions.

Process observations from scan, navigation, and look-for calls are uniformly sampled into at most eight frames for observation maintenance; the policy uses the latest four available frames. Verification uses the existing immediate pre- and post-action frames, the request, and expected effects, without implicitly moving the camera. When QA is triggered, the same model answers in a dedicated turn using the question and the policy context, including the current instruction, images, public request history, agenda, routed memory, and control context; it outputs only the answer.

J.2 Agenda Representation and Updates

Each agenda item stores a stable identifier, requirement, mode, status, evidence references, and optional next intent. Modes are required, ongoing, or conditional; statuses are pending, active, watching, supported, or blocked, indicating outstanding work, current focus, awaiting relevant evidence, evidence satisfying the current criterion, or a missing prerequisite. The agenda contains at most eight items with at most one active item; item order does not prescribe execution order.

Supported status is interpreted according to the requirement. A state inspection is supported when the requested information is observed; an execution requirement is supported when visual verification establishes its intended effect; an ongoing constraint is supported only for the current state and remains monitored. Discovering that a condition holds activates the associated work without establishing its fulfillment. Request history and temporary planning assumptions cannot independently support completion. Later observations contradicting supporting evidence reopen affected items.

Changes in public task requirements or relevant committed memory trigger revision rather than rewriting the agenda at every call. Prompts ask the model to propose task-scoped additions, necessary prerequisites, recovery needs, and duplicate merging; the commit layer checks fields, identifiers, references, and evidence eligibility for supported status. The model judges task relevance and semantic duplication; deterministic validation enforces the record structure and evidence requirements. The agenda advises the policy without directly defining action admissibility.

Initialization establishes explicit requirements and conditional inspection needs from the instruction. Unresolved inspection items and next intents guide the policy’s choice of observation tools and targets. New public instructions are incorporated into task context; either instruction changes or relevant memory changes trigger agenda revision. QA questions are not treated as additional task requirements.

For a task to inspect a kitchen and turn off running faucets, initialization establishes an inspection need and a conditional shutoff requirement. Observing running water creates a scene fact and activates shutoff work without creating a failure incident. The shutoff requirement becomes supported only when post-action visual evidence establishes that flow has stopped. Continued flow instead records an execution incident and preserves outstanding work. Discovering one faucet does not automatically complete an inspection covering the entire kitchen.

J.3 Memory Maintenance and Routing

Facts store an identifier, public subject, property or relation, value, confidence, frame and action references, observation step, and validity status: current, stale, or contradicted. These fields inform the model’s semantic judgments, while deterministic routines enforce record consistency and manage memory storage and routing. Incidents store an identifier, source action, discrepancy type, evidence, creation and update steps, handling status, and recovery attempts. Obligations store an identifier, observe or act type, relevant public objects, optional source incident, creation step, and open or resolved status.

Pre-decision observation maintenance distinguishes discovery from reconciliation. Discovery adds visible objects and conditions as scene-observation facts without independently creating incidents or obligations. Reconciliation assigns candidate facts a confirmed, contradicted, unobservable, or unknown assessment. Confirmation refreshes supporting evidence; contradiction marks a fact as contradicted; unobservable and unknown assessments alone do not authorize negation. A newer scene description of the same subject can supersede an earlier one. Proposals reference the relevant facts and images; the commit layer checks memory revision, reference existence, evidence eligibility, and consistency between assessments and mutations before commitment.

Default capacity is 64 facts, 16 incidents, and 16 obligations; routed context contains at most six facts, two incidents, and three obligations. Fact ordering first prioritizes currently relevant objects, then penalizes scene observations unrelated to the instruction, and then favors recent observations with stable identifiers breaking ties. Currently relevant objects come from unresolved needs and recent public interaction targets. Incidents prioritize unresolved entries and newer creation times; obligations prioritize unresolved entries and older creation times. Routing preserves validity and evidence references to distinguish historical records from current evidence.

Capacity maintenance preferentially removes stale facts and resolved records; unresolved incidents and obligations cannot be treated as handled through silent deletion. Post-action effect commitment complements pre-decision observation maintenance: the former records verification outcomes and corresponding recovery needs, while the latter handles additions and contradictions from later observations without readjudicating the same before/after evidence.

J.4 Verification, Recovery, and Planning Assumptions

Requests record selected actions, admission determines whether they may execute, and visual verification assesses their effects. The evaluator separately determines task success under Appendix A.4; control decisions and budget exhaustion do not establish success.

Verification success indicates visual support for the intended effect, failure indicates an observable discrepancy, and ambiguity indicates insufficient evidence. Outputs include evidence and observability assessments; occlusion or a lack of obvious image change does not automatically establish failure. Success commits only supported effects; failure creates or updates incidents and associated obligations; ambiguity preserves unconfirmed effects and requests observation when needed.

Recovery state contains the original request, target, expected effect, evidence, handling phase, and remaining attempts. The controller can require observation, approach, prerequisite satisfaction, or retry. For placement recovery, held, released, and unknown respectively call for returning toward the destination, localization and pickup, or further observation first. Effects of recovery calls remain subject to verification.

If uncertainty persists after bounded observation or retry, recovery branches that permit continuation may retain temporary planning assumptions. These reside in recovery or control context, cannot be committed as verified facts, and cannot support agenda completion. An explicitly observed failure cannot be assumed successful; subsequent evidence may revise or revoke an assumption. Terminal branches end execution with unresolved state retained.

J.5 Anti-Deadlock Control and Execution Order

The exploration ledger groups scans, searches, and navigation by room or semantic target and tracks observation and preparation calls without advancing interaction. At the corresponding limits, the controller rejects repetitive candidates before execution, supplies a reselection reason, and restricts tools, promoting approach and then interaction where appropriate. Relevant new evidence or admitted physical calls reset the corresponding counters under the control rules; precondition-rejected calls and changes in timestamps or step indices do not.

Recovery observations, retries of the original action, and model reselection each have finite budgets. Controller-required recovery calls take precedence over ordinary action selection, with the agenda serving as policy context. QA uses dedicated answer turns outside exploration candidate selection. Execution, answer, and stop requests each consume a high-level step; internal model calls and reselection do not add environment steps.

Default control limits.

Within a no-progress phase, the default limits are two scans, two searches and two navigation calls per semantic target, four observation calls in total, and six observation/navigation preparation calls in total. A rejected candidate permits at most two additional model reselection requests. Recovery contexts default to two retry rounds, while dedicated placement recovery additionally permits at most eight recovery actions. These limits apply within their respective ledgers and do not extend the episode’s environment-step budget.

Exhausted dedicated placement recovery terminates with a control failure. Generic recovery branches that permit continuation retain unconfirmed state and separately marked planning assumptions. Later evidence revises these assumptions.

Algorithm 1 orders observation maintenance, agenda revision, routing, action selection, and effect commitment; Algorithm 2 details bounded action selection. MM denotes memory, AA the agenda, RR recovery state, LL the control ledger, HH public request history, and WW the available image buffer. Calls parameterized by θ\theta share the same model; other operations perform deterministic control or environment interaction.

Observe comprises discovery and reconciliation with their respective update permissions. RecentRequests retains up to 48 public requests; policy and QA calls share context κ\kappa. UpdateRecovery maintains phases, budgets, and permitted planning assumptions. Agenda acceptance checks structure, references, and evidence eligibility, while the model handles task scope and semantic merging.

XX contains the initial instruction and subsequent public task messages, while EE tracks processed image identifiers. Task updates exclude QA questions and can trigger agenda revision without waiting for a new visual fact.

Updated recovery state and control ledgers are returned to the main loop.

Memory maintenance tracks frame identifiers and update responsibilities. A post-action image can support discovery of other scene information, while its action-effect assessment is committed through verification. Repeated frames retain their existing evidence identity.

Appendix K Execution Trace Visualization

The simulated execution traces in Figure 4 and this section are produced by Qwen3.8-27B with SCOPER-harness. Some redundant intermediate exploration steps and frames are omitted for readability. Real-data examples illustrate next-tool-call evaluation conditioned on reference execution prefixes.

Execution failures and disturbances.

Figure 5 shows a misplaced plant pot being located, retrieved, and placed correctly. Figure 6 illustrates retrieval after a slipped grasp, while Figure 7 shows visual search and corrected navigation after reaching the wrong target. Figure 8 illustrates inspection and retry after a partial drawer opening. Figures 9 and 10 follow a two-object storage task: after storing the first object, the cabinet closes again and must be reopened before storing the second.

Observation-dependent requirements and action dependencies.

Figures 11 and 12 show discovery of a dirty mug followed by cleaning and storage. Figure 13 illustrates a safety inspection in which observations identify a running faucet and an open fridge. Figures 14 and 15 show observation of a dirty bowl activating the instruction-specified cleaning and storage requirement during a tomato-placement task. Figure 16 illustrates sequential dependencies: the knife must be put down after slicing before the apple slices can be picked up and placed.

Real-observation decision nodes.

Figure 17 illustrates movement and reinspection revealing evidence relevant to the next action, such as a fallen cushion or remaining litter. Figure 18 illustrates synthetic early-stop decision nodes: picking, placing, opening, or approaching is still incomplete at the marked endpoint. These are imposed truncations of reference demonstrations, rather than recorded execution malfunctions. Later reference frames illustrate eventual outcomes and are excluded from model inputs.

Appendix L Harness Model-Call Overhead

Direct execution uses one model call per high-level step. SCOPER adds role-specific calls around action selection: the policy usually makes one call per step; discovery makes one call when new images are available; reconciliation makes one call when existing facts can be checked; agenda revision makes one call when the instruction or committed memory changes; and the verifier makes one call after an admitted operation requiring outcome verification. These calls support action selection, acquisition of new scene facts, assessment of earlier evidence, task-progress updates, and visual outcome checks, respectively. Averaged over evaluation on the complete 870-task benchmark, SCOPER uses approximately 3.7×3.7\times as many model calls as direct execution. Internal calls do not add environment-interaction steps; both methods retain the same high-level step budgets.
